paragraphs: In the winter of Yuanxing’s second year, more than half the reeds along the Fei River had turned yellow and dry. A light frost had fallen in the night. Morning mist floated above the water, revealing its dark blue-green only where the current ran fast. On the official road south of Shouyang came first the dull thud of iron-shod hooves in mud, then the grating of wagon wheels on gravel. Scouts from Former Qin reached the bank, dismounted to sound the water, and planted a small vermilion flag on a rise.

The camps halted in the order marked by the flags. Cavalry circled to the western heights, river troops descended into the branching channels to test the water, and grain wagons headed first toward designated storage grounds to the north rather than crowd the road with marching infantry. Junior clerks holding tally boards checked one unit after another beside the road. If one battalion was late, they left a gap between its neighbors so the rear columns would not mistake the empty place for men deserting on the eve of battle. Soldiers and horses flowed steadily through the white fog. Even by noon there had been no drumbeats of confusion.

The previous autumn Fu Jian had authorized fifty thousand soldiers to proceed to the northern Huai to investigate appeals for aid. Once winter began, he assigned another thirty thousand as reserves from existing garrisons in Henan and east of the passes; the Secretariat and army command verified every transfer against its roll. The vanguard had not suddenly become a million-man army conscripting all the able-bodied men of the north. Only troops needed to guard the river could camp nearest the Fei; the others took turns repairing roads and guarding provisions north of Shouyang. Young generals thought the arrangement slow. It prevented many of the quarrels that once followed armies seizing ground for camps along their route.

A family hid in a ruined shrine by the river. An old woman held a small child in her arms; a millstone with a broken leg leaned inside the doorway. Her husband had once piloted boats for the Jin army, and later carried bolts of hemp cloth for the Huan troops. After he was injured and lost his wages, the couple had been forced to shelter in the shrine. Hearing soldiers approach outside, she buried her rice jar in the hearth ashes, afraid someone would once again open the door and demand food.

But a passing detachment leader first planted a wooden board in front of the shrine and pointed out its unit number and prohibitions. The old woman could not read. He tapped the two spots of white paint on his armored shoulder and told her that if anyone seized her grain, she should report to the blue tent to the north. Hearing the soldier speak with a stiff accent from the Jiang–Huai country, the child could not resist asking, “Are you from the south too?”
“My mother is in Hedong,” the leader said. “My father came from the lands of Yan. These days my name is on the military rolls at Luoyang.”

The child wanted to ask more, but the man picked up his leather waterskin and went on. The old woman gazed at the board beside her doorway for a long while, hesitating, and still did not dig up her rice jar. She had seen too many prohibitions written on wooden boards to believe a plank could save a family. Yet she had also watched this soldier walk around the fence without taking even the bundle of firewood drying beneath the eaves.

Fu Jian arrived as the sun neared its height. He wore none of his old jeweled armor, only a dark padded robe with a short fur cloak, and rode in a broad-shafted army carriage. Years of lingering illness had left his right knee unable to endure jolting. At every post house the attendants prepared hot water first, and thick felt lined the carriage. Behind him a military clerk carried the medicine chest. The scent of herbs mingled with axle grease, a smell that had become familiar on journeys with the sovereign.

At the riverbank he asked to get down. Fu Rong reached out without a word of protest. Taking his brother’s wrist, Fu Jian stepped onto the ground. The moment his boot touched the wet mud, cold pierced through the sole to the very bone of his knee.
“The river has changed its course,” Fu Jian said.
“Three times in twenty years.” Fu Rong pointed upstream. “Our old camp stood beyond that ridge. Mulberry fields cover it now.”

They walked slowly along the sand. Fu Rong’s temples had whitened early, and his left shoulder ached in cold and damp; beneath the cloak he could scarcely raise that arm. Twenty years earlier, when they had stood at the Fei River, almost no one believed the army of a million on the rolls would finally turn north without crossing. Fu Jian had looked south for a long time, believing the Yangtze and Jiankang lay only one stretch of water, one military order, away. But each Qin formation then had its own familiar banners, its grain was levied hurriedly from every quarter, and once its men lost their commander they could scatter into the old territories of their separate peoples.

Now shards of ice covered the shallows. Bridge piles left from the previous year had rotted, and the Qin army had brought new ropes and floating timbers. Commands had changed as well. Young Xianbei horsemen received grain against their military tallies. Veteran Qiang soldiers served in the same battalion as Han troops from Guanzhong. Whoever damaged a house by the river had to pay for it; no one first asked which tribe or command he had belonged to. Yet Fu Jian knew that men whom military law had barely managed to gather together over the years still carried their clans and former kingdoms within them. New registers had altered the way they obtained land and rations, but could not necessarily erase the wounds passed down by their grandfathers.

He stopped beside the water. His toe touched half an arrowhead. It was thick with muddy rust; nothing remained to show whether Qin or Jin had forged it. Fu Jian had it washed, turned it over in his hands for a while, then told a guard to place it back where it had lain.
“It may not be from that year,” Fu Rong said.
“There have been many battles on this river since.”

Fu Jian sat on a blue-gray stone by the bank. The ten years Wang Meng had asked for from his deathbed were long past. Most of the generals who had once urged him not to cross the Fei were themselves buried in scattered northern graves. Fu Hong had managed state affairs in his stead for years. Officials now dared to return improper edicts for revision in open court, and Yao Chang’s rising two years earlier had not torn Guanzhong apart into tribal factions. Fu Jian had lived through these changes and knew how painfully they had been won. In bringing an army south once more, he did not intend to let one reckless victory or defeat destroy them all.

Hoofbeats sounded in the distance. A captain reported that the Northern Garrison had formed ranks on the southern bank, perhaps twenty thousand men visible around the shallows, with towns and villages delivering grain behind them; the exact number was uncertain. Alongside the Jin flags they displayed a great banner of black characters on white. Only after climbing into a tree could the scouts make out its four words: The South Saves Itself.

Fu Rong frowned. The very claim to rule all under Heaven was being thrown into confusion between Jiankang and Jingzhou, yet Liu Yu had raised a new banner beside Jin’s. Had a Qin commander presumed to do such a thing, both military law and the court would have demanded to know his intentions. Fu Jian passed no judgment. He ordered a sketch made of the flag and sent with the other reports to the central tent.

The defenses were complete by afternoon. Qin did not connect every palisade into an unbroken wall. Wide lanes between camps remained open for grain wagons and carts bearing the wounded. The flotilla occupied the river branches alone, cavalry held the heights, and reserve grain was kept clear of low ground near the water. Account clerks laid wooden tally sticks in rows. When a granary opened, each captain entered in the order of his unit number; anyone drawing one extra sack had to produce a written authorization for the supplement.

Some veterans could not accustom themselves to this. On earlier southern campaigns, entering a county had been enough to levy its horses and grain. Now even a pontoon bridge required verification of whether the trees to be felled stood on state land or private fields; even water drawn from a well had to be entered in the expense book. A young deputy general joked that there were more clerks in the army than crossbowmen. Before nightfall his men chased Jin scouts into a village by mistake and led away two chickens. Camp inspectors hauled them to the central command for a flogging, then returned the chickens and a grain receipt to their owner. The deputy’s smile vanished.

Yet the following day someone accused a Qin soldier of injuring a southerner on the road. The soldier claimed the man had been spying on military routes; the southerner said he was only searching for his missing daughter. Both sides had witnesses. By supper their quarrel had reached the army headquarters. Fu Jian heard the accounts and ordered the accused soldier confined and the injured man examined by a physician; the man’s identity would be investigated separately. He would not let irritation decide for the law which account was true. War had not yet begun, and already many people had been hurt here.

From a watchtower on the southern shore, Liu Yu was looking over the Qin camp. He wore old lamellar armor, its breastplates repaired twice, and the mouth of his sword scabbard was worn pale. In summer he had crossed north to visit the wounded. He and Fu Hong had carried sick men together through a flooded camp, and someone had given him a pair of dry boots. He wore them now, their soles scuffed and roughened by the mud of the south.

Liu Muzhi stood beside him. Just back from the rear camp, he reported that three fortified estates would supply grain, but only if the Northern Garrison assigned five hundred soldiers to guard their gates. Liu Yu asked whether the households would admit nearby refugees into their compounds. Two refused, Liu Muzhi said. One offered empty rooms but forbade the guests to approach its granary.

“If I leave our men at their gates, who holds the gap in our line?” Liu Yu pointed to the western reed flats. “Tell them to open their stores and lend grain first, and let civilians shelter within their walls. I will send mounted patrols to guard the road to the main crossing. If they still refuse, they will not get a single one of those five hundred men.”

Liu Muzhi recorded the instructions but did not immediately leave. He glanced at the two banners high on the southern bank. Wind and rain had frayed the four edges of the Jin flag. The white banner had only lately been sewn; the characters for “The South Saves Itself” stood a little crooked, the last one cramped almost against the edge.
“The men in Jiankang may not like it,” said Liu Muzhi.
“Huan Xuan will like it even less.”
“Then why does the general keep the Jin flag?”

Liu Yu descended two rungs of the watchtower ladder and stopped. He had heard too much advice that year. Some said the Jin house was no longer worth defending. Some said the north would receive refugees, so they might as well admit Qin troops. Others asked why anyone should die for a handful of aristocratic clans: keep your own army safe and let the rest go. He had seen northern camps open their gates by night to save the sick. He had also seen aged soldiers in the south, unpaid for months, carry confiscated civilian grain back to its village. He would not use any banner to declare, in advance, that all these people belonged to someone else.
“The old flag is still here,” said Liu Yu. “The debt to those who died beneath it has not been settled.”
Liu Muzhi offered no further counsel. He had a second grain shipment to hurry along. Before leaving he said, “Fu Jian is old, but his army clerks understand better than ours how to hold a road.”
“Then learn more from them,” Liu Yu said, looking across to the northern shore. “Do not stop at making the camps look impressive.”

The wind off the river strengthened. Northern Garrison soldiers drove stakes into the shallows while men on boats tested old submerged ropes with iron hooks. Ox carts came in rotation from village communities. Those bringing grain included tenants of great houses and army dependents owed months of pay. They were strangers to one another, yet all pressed their fingerprints onto the same distribution register. Liu Yu knew they would quarrel over land taxes again tomorrow. Today their grain and labor were what sustained his army.

When Fu Jian climbed the northern watchtower, Murong Chui was already seated there. Wrapped in thick felt, the old general’s face was so pale it seemed nearly transparent. His fingers trembled slightly from years of old injuries. Before he left Ye, men of his former clan had urged him to claim illness and retire. Why follow the Fu family south yet again? He had simply asked for the iron saddle he had used decades before and ordered a craftsman to mend its broken clasp. The imperial emblems of old Yan had once almost lured him home. But the flooded city of Ye had taught him that living people had no time left to wait for the return of a ruler from a dead dynasty.

Fu Jian told him not to rise. Facing each other, the two men could see deeper lines in each other’s faces than at their last meeting. Fu Rong spread out a plan of the formations opposite. Jin river stockades stood apart among the tributaries; the forward camp had three lines of crossbows, and the grain wagons were not concentrated in one place. Behind them, fortified estates that plainly competed for advantage were nevertheless willing to send provisions down a single road.

A young commander declared that the southern force was small and would surely break within two days of a concentrated crossing. Murong Chui had someone help him to his feet and walked to the railing. He looked out for a long moment. “To break the line in front, perhaps two days is too many. What happens after that?”
“We march on Jiankang.”
“On what boats? Who guards every landing along the river? Which household feeds your vanguard? And the fortified estates you pass by: to whom will they open their gates at night?”
The commander replied that Qin had already issued its Compact for Crossing the River; naturally its soldiers would not trouble the people. Murong Chui glanced toward Fu Jian and shook his head.

“The men who wrote the compact are in Chang’an. The people who must see it honored are here. Between them lies a river and half a lifetime of war and hatred. Even if northern soldiers truly obey the rules, someone must still be willing to believe them.”

Fu Jian handed the young commander a viewing tube and ordered him to study the grain wagons behind the southern line. At first he counted only banners and soldiers. Then he noticed several women near the wagons holding infants while handing water to the men. Farther back, villagers were repairing a road along the field ridges; they carried no blades.
“If Liu Yu is defeated and retreats,” Fu Jian asked, “what will happen to those people?”

They would scatter, the commander said. Fu Jian asked how many would flee toward the Qin camp and how many hide in the hills; where grain might be bought and where it could only be taken by force. The commander held the viewing tube without an answer. Fu Jian ordered him to return to the heights the following day. His report must list the likely movements of the civilians separately. A count of warboats and crossbows alone did not make a complete map of the field.

Zhu Xu was on the watchtower too. He had come from Jiankang to mediate along the Huai, crossing the river with only letters entrusted to him by villagers and private messages from former Xiangyang comrades, not an official Qin seal. Some in Huan Xuan’s administration still called him a friend of Qin, while men in Qin’s army suspected he carried messages for Liu Yu. He made excuses for neither side. When someone asked what gave Liu Yu the right to raise a banner saying “The South Saves Itself,” Zhu Xu answered only that Liu Yu had once allowed Qin grain into a Jin city and had faced interrogation for releasing an officer who had brought grain to save civilians. He would tell southerners what was good about Qin, but would not for that reason hand over the Jin army’s command tally.

Murong Chui smiled at this, then the smile turned to a small cough. Fu Jian asked how Liu Yu’s men compared with Xie Xuan’s twenty years earlier. The old general studied the opposite bank and answered that Xie Xuan’s formations had been more precise, while Liu Yu had far fewer men at his command. Xie Xuan also had the Xie family and his reputation in Jiankang behind him. Liu Yu had yet to win over all the Northern Garrison veterans. He paused to steady his breathing, then added: precisely for that reason, every victory Liu Yu won would teach his followers who apportioned their grain, buried their dead, and paid what they were owed.
“And if he loses?” Fu Rong asked.
“Huan Xuan is waiting for him to lose as well,” Murong Chui replied. “If he does, those soldiers may have nowhere left to go.”
Fu Jian turned toward him. “Do you think I should let him win?”
“I know only this: if he is willing to stand here and defend the crossing, his people will not lay down their swords overnight merely because we promise them a few good laws.”

Fu Jian held the railing for a long time. Across the Fei, the lights were much sparser than in the Qin camp, yet because the positions were scattered, they flickered in and out of the field mist. He remembered Wang Meng’s counsel at his deathbed. He remembered how many people had sincerely believed Yao Chang’s proclamations when he rose in Guanzhong. He thought of Murong Chui refusing former ministers in the old Yan palace, and how Liang Agui’s name had once appeared beside the Chang’an appointment notices, linked to an arrow loosed at the Heavenly King. A government could be repaired. No single edict could set every heart in order.

Before sunset, scouting boats from opposite banks met midstream. Both sides had crossbows cocked. The Qin captain mistook the Jin boat for one probing the channel and ordered his craft to rush forward. A red lantern rose at once above the southern river stockade. Seeing the Qin vessel pass its agreed boundary marker, the northern river-patrol commander repeatedly signaled it to withdraw. As the fast boat turned back, the Jin crew still had time to shoot. Instead, they beat a single stroke on their drum and let it go.

On hearing the report, Fu Jian asked who had ordered the boat withdrawn. Told that the river-patrol commander had acted under the new regulations, he ordered a commendation entered. Liu Yu also demanded to know why the Jin crew had not fired. Their captain said the Qin boat had lowered its signal and retreated; to shoot first would put the southern grain boats at risk. Liu Yu told him to teach the grain porters to distinguish military flags and warned the night watch against giving way to passing anger. By the time word reached both armies, dusk had fallen. Many soldiers never even learned that three loaded crossbows had briefly faced one another on the river.

After nightfall Fu Rong brought Fu Jian hot broth. Finding his elder brother still on the high platform, his fur cloak ballooning in the wind, he urged him to return to the tent. Fu Jian pointed to the southern bank and asked what they would have done with the south if, twenty years ago, they had struck Xie Xuan’s army while it was halfway across and won.

Fu Rong was silent for a long time. They would have entered Jiankang, he said, awarded honors, and stationed their various armies in the commanderies. But the Qin troops of those days lacked today’s military registration and supply system. The northern garrisons had not been brought to order either. Who could have stopped commanders from using military merit to fight for newly conquered lands? Who could have delivered grain to both banks of the Yangtze on time? He could not say.
“Things are better today,” Fu Jian said.
“Much better,” Fu Rong answered.
“But the people opposite us have changed as well.”

Fu Rong looked toward the river and slowly understood that his elder brother did not want to stake twenty years of work on the simple outcome of one battle. Yet generals in the empire still longed to cross, and civilians in the south still begged for troops. Every time the army slowed, someone waited for grain, waited for medicine, or failed to live to see another day. The brothers sat side by side. Neither spoke lightly.

Deep in the night a small boat bearing a white flag came slowly from the southern shore. The Qin river camp sounded its bronze gong twice, followed by the challenge for examining military letters. Three people were aboard with a sealed wooden casket. The night watch escorted them to the outer corridor of headquarters and verified that Liu Yu had sent them. They asked to present the letter that night and deliver their formal statement before the command in the morning.

Inside the casket lay a chart of the waterways and a short letter in Liu Yu’s own hand. Its words were plain: the remaining Huan factions in the south had yet to be suppressed; the Northern Garrison needed to use the channels near the Fei to return its troops; the Qin camp held the crossings, the two armies stood opposed, and each extra day consumed more grain from the people. Liu Yu asked Qin to move its camp thirty li north temporarily so the southern troops could pass. Each side would set boundary markers, and neither would pursue the other without cause for five days. His pen strokes at the close were so heavy that the ink showed through the paper.

At the words “thirty li,” an attendant general almost struck the corner off the table. In his understanding of imperial might, the enemy should always be the first to give ground. Nearly eighty thousand Qin soldiers now held positions throughout the Jiang–Huai region, while only several tens of thousands of Northern Garrison men stood to the south, yet they dared ask the Heavenly King to withdraw his camp. Fu Jian did not silence him. He first ordered the waterways and grain-cart routes shown on the chart examined for accuracy.

The Northern Garrison envoy stood beneath the eaves, pale-faced, rain dripping from his sleeves into the cracks between the stones. His commander, he said, would pledge his complete grain accounts, the names of the boats, and the route of return. If a single unit strayed from its assigned crossing, Qin could demand an explanation. Someone asked why Liu Yu trusted Qin not to strike his rear while it drew back. The envoy answered slowly: “The general said that only because the north has been able to keep its compact does he dare ask this.”

Fu Jian set the letter beneath a lamp and read it word by word. He did not order the camps moved in the night, nor did he send the envoy away. Instead, he had a secretary record Liu Yu’s five days, thirty li, and each waterway for the council. He summoned Fu Rong and Murong Chui to examine the proposal overnight, and would hear the envoy’s statement in person after dawn.

Wind shook the candle flames. Drops of wax fell near the edge of the map. Fu Jian pressed a corner of the paper flat with his hand. Suddenly the two characters for Fei River, set at the center of the crossing routes drawn in blue ink, looked like a crease someone had left twenty years earlier. He had stopped a great battle here once. Now a new general born in the south asked him to move back thirty li. Liu Yu had no imperial seal and no full court of ministers to endorse him. He had only a few camps and the grain delivered to him by the riverside people with which to bargain with the Heavenly King of the north.

Fu Jian ordered an attendant to bring a fresh lamp and set it beside the chart. Clear light spread across the tributaries, flats, and camp roads of both banks. The council had not dispersed; the sky was still dark. The white-flag envoy was lodged in the forward tent to await the morning hearing.
Beyond the watchtower, the fires of Qin and the Northern Garrison faced one another across the water. The river ran past the broken piles of the old bridge, making no announcement, never pausing.
